speechtext: I see by a British Columbia newspaper that the provincial government is taking up the question of building hatcheries. Is there any conflict of jurisdiction on this subject between the Dominion and the province ?

The hon. gentleman knows that we have not yet finally and definitely settled the question which has arisen out of the celebrated decision given by the Privy Council in the fisheries case, that is, the exact point where the jurisdiction of the Dominion ends and the jurisdiction of the province begins. It has been settled satisfactorily that the rivers and lakes are the property of the provincial government, and carry the property in the fish, and they alone have the right to license the exclusive locations to fishermen in those lakes and rivers. But when you come to the sea-coast a different question arises* and we

have been endeavouring to arrange a case with the maritime provinces and Quebec for submission to the Privy Council, to find out just where the jurisdiction of the province ends and the jurisdiction of the Dominion begins. Onr contention is that the jurisdiction of the province ends and the jurisdiction of the Dominion begins at low-water mark. There is in that sense a conflict of jurisdiction ; but there is no active conflict. We have so far carried on our fishing business and enforced our regulations in British Columbia without any opposition whatever from the British Columbia government.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: This paper states that the local government propose to establish two fish hatcheries on the Fraser river, at a cost of $7,000 each. I understand that this vote is to establish a fish hatchery ou the same river ?

To complete it. We have had a fish hatchery on the Fraser river, at New Westminster, for many years ; but it became old and obsolete, and at the request of the members from British Columbia, we took a vote to build a new one further up the river. It is quite possible that the provincial government may supplement our efforts in that direction by building hatcheries of their own. Of course, we could not and would not prevent that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: It is evident that both the Dominion and the provincial governments are engaging in the same work. I am not objecting to that ; but, I want to use it as a precedent, and ask the minister if he would not do the same act of kindness towards us in the Georgian Bay district, where most of the ova for whitefish and salmon-trout have been collected for years, and where there are excellent facilities, say on the Beaver river, for establishing a fish hatchery in the very locality where the ova are collected. I have brought this matter before the House repeatedly during the last twenty years, but I have never yet been able to induce the government to take it up. If the minister can justify this expenditure in British Columbia, where the local government are doing it for themselves, surely he ought to go further and do it in the other provinces as well. If he does that, there is no place better entitled to it than the Georgian Bay district, where the ova are collected and brought down here to be hatched out.

I think there is a great deal in what my hon. friend says. The matter has been under consideration, and favourable consideration ; and I am strongly impressed with the desirability of doing what he suggests ; but he knows how difficult it is to get all you apply for in council. I am personally in favour of building a fish hatchery on the Georgian Bay. I think it is the
proper place for one. I have always thought it was unfortunate that the hatchery was placed at Newcastle by the late Mr. W'ilmot. I think it is the wrong place. So far as I am concerned, if a new hatchery is to be built in Ontario, it will be built in the Georgian Bay. That is my opinion, and the opinion of the officers of my department. It is my intention this year to propose a vote for a biological fish laboratory in the Georgian Bay for the study of fish life. The fish life of the Georgian Bay is one of the most valuable we have in Canada, and we know very little of the habits of the fish living in those waters. The suggestion which the hon. gentleman makes, I frankly say, has my sympathy, and I hope it will be carried out; but he knows I cannot get all I want to get.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I hope the hon. minister's efforts in convincing his colleagues will be successful. I am sure the people in that district would appreciate it very much.

May I ask on what principle the hon. minister is working this combined lobster and salmon hatchery in GaspS? Will he take the different fish in different seasons, and utilize the one hatchery for hatching out both kinds of fish-the salmon in the fall and the lobsters in the spring and summer ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I think it is a capital idea.
Mr. Prince, the commissioner of fisheries, has worked it out pretty thoroughly, and I believe it will be a grand success.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman be able to do anything towards that fishery he speaks of in the Georgian Bay ? I have had a request from Prof. Louden and those associated with him in the formation of a club at the mouth of the Pene-tanguishene. They are very anxious to get a small grant for the purpose of establishing a hatchery such as the hon. gentleman has been speaking of.
I think I can give my hon. friend the assurance that that will be done, but as the estimates are not down I cannot speak positively.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I would call the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that we had a salmon hatchery on Prince Edward Island a few years ago, which was unfortunately burned down. The government still hold the site of that hatchery, which proved to be a great success. In view of the fact that the lobster fishery is one of great importance around the coast, I trust that the hon. minister, if he cannot do anything this

session, will see his way next session to build on that site a general hatchery such as he proposes to build at Gasp6. If the site be too far up the river, it might be moved further down where he would have fresh and salt water.
Department of Agriculture-Salaries, $330.

The first increase is not a statutory increase, but an indemnity given to Mr. Jarvis, secretary of the department, who has had to do the work of the deputy as well as his own, the deputy having unfortunately been ill. I thought it only fair to allow Mr. Jarvis some recognition for his work.
Experimental Fai;ms, $1,500.
This is due to a larger distribution of the bulletins and reports. Prof. Saunders says he has now three bulletins ready to issue which ought to be in the hands of the farmers.
What are those bulletins ?
One is on the cultivation of the apple, now ready for the printer. One is about clover and its value as a fertilizer, and one is on soft pork.
Is there any regular system for the bringing out and distribution of these bulletins ?

They are issued whenever the experiments of the farm have reached a point to justify conclusions being drawn. The bulletins are the accumulated results of these experiments, brought together and worked out by an officer in charge of the experiments, and are the opinion and judgment of that officer supervised by the director.
How many are distributed, and to whom ?

The mail list of farmers comprises some 50,000. Some bulletins are of general application and go out to the whole of the mail list, while some go only to specialists. For instance, we have a list of horticulturists and orchardists, and the orchard bulletin would go only to these and probably to the farmers in the fruit-growing districts, but not to the whole 50,000 on the mailing list. The bulletin with regard to the raising of soft pork would go to all.

How are the lists made up ? Some years ago, I understand, the mailing list consisted of members of farmers' institutes, in addition to such names as have been handed in by the member for the district. But I do not know whether they were continued year after year regardless of whether these people continued to be members of institutes or not. On one occasion the members of the House revised Mr. HACKETT.
the lists for their several constituencies, but that seems to be done only once in a great many years. Is the same system kept up now, or from what source are the names drawn to fill the lists from time to time ?

The lists are chiefly filled up from two sources. The first of these is the correspondence received at the farm. We have many applications from all parts of the country for information of various kinds, and the writers generally ask to be put upon the mailing lists, which is done. Then, members of the House recommend names to be put upon the mailing list. We find that the list must be gone over because men move, and their post offices are no longer correct, some die, and so on-there is a constant slight revision of that kind. I think that once since I came into office we have had a complete revision of the mailing list, each county list being gone over and corrected.

I thought it was before the hon. gentleman came into office that that revision was made. The lists were revised a great many years ago, each member of the House revising the list for his own constituency. Many of us found on the list names of men who had died or moved away ten or twelve years before. The lists were very imperfect, and thus a great deal of the literature was thrown away. I would suggest a revision of the lists every few years, and it seems to me that the method that I have suggested is the most effective. We were told that we might send in a number of names-I think it was 200 from each constituency. I think that that ought to be enlarged and that members ought to have the privilege from year to year of adding to that list, and of revising the list every few years.

It seems to me that the system of distribution is very uncertain and that a minimum of good is gained by the distribution made. The cost of the experimental farm seems to be about $80,000 a year, while the cost of distribution is about $4,000 a year. This distribution reaches about 50,000, or about one-tenth of the farmers of the country. Seeing that the farm costs so much, it seems to me that it would be more economical to increase the distribution. If the information gained as the result of the $80,000 of expenditure is a good thing for 50,000 farmers, it would be a good thing for 50,000 more. I think the distribution should be more extensive if it is a good thing to gain and distribute this valuable information to 50,000 farmers at an expense of $84,000, surely it would be a good thing to distribute the same information to another 50,000 farmers at an expense of only $4,000 or so, and so on until all of the 50,000 farmers of Canada received the same information that this favoured few

received now. It may be that those who receive them now are among the most progressive farmers-that depends upon how the names are obtained, to whom these bulletins are sent; but surely the 45,000 farmers who do not receive these bulletins now and to whom they might be sent at an expense less than the present cost of gaining and distributing the information to less than 50,000 would receive in the aggregate much more information and the country would be benefited to a much greater extent for this additional expenditure than it is by that now made.

It is well understood, and has been published over and over again all over the country, that anybody who applies for this literature will have his name placed upon the list and will receive it. The number of names on the list is really the number of those who apply. The fact that any one may receive this literature has been announced at all sorts of agricultural meetings, it has been advertised over and over again not only in the agricultural press, but in the weekly press and in many other ways. I do not mean that we put in paid advertisements, but I mean that the fact is constanly referred to in articles, editorials and communications which are sent to the newspapers. The result of that widespread advertisement is that about 50,000 have applied. If 50,000 more would apply, the literature would be sent to them-but in that case, of course, I should be obliged to ask for more money. The list has varied a little year by year, and names have been changed, but the list has kept at about the same size. I do not think that there is anybody who wants this literature who does not receive it. I would be very glad indeed if more people would ask for it.
Are there any records kept of how many of the 50,000 have applied in their own names ? Are there not a large number sent in by friends, by members of parliament, and so on ?
None of this literature is sent out by members of parliament, it is all sent out from the farm.
I did not mean that-I meant sent at the request of members of parliament and others.

Yes; if a member of parliament sends in a reasonable number of names-and I have never fixed a limit-these names would certainly be put upon the list. This is being done constantly. Members every now and again ask to see the lists for their own counties and correct and add to them.
Has the hon. minister any literature ready for distribution now ?

I think there are two bulletins now in the press. But I would like the hon. gentleman to understand that this literature goes from the farm direct, and is not sent to the members of the House for distribution. If the hon. member wants it sent to people in his own county he should send in a list, and the documents will be sent to the people he names.

Can the hon. minister give us what percentage of those on the list receive the farm report of the Minister of Agriculture and the report of experimental farms ? As I understand it, some years ago an arrangement was made between the Dominion Minister of Agriculture and the provincial Minister of Agriculture that those belonging to farmers' institutes were to receive a copy of the farm report or the farm bulletins. Does he know what percentage of these will receive the farm report ?

We do not accept the names of members of any associations of that kind; that is, we do* not take the list of names sent in by a secretary. The farmers' institutes grew to such large proportions that it was practically impossible to do it. Besides, the institutes' membership changed greatly every year. If such an arrangement as the hon. gentleman speaks of was carried out some years ago, and I dare say it was, it had fallen to the ground before I came into office.
Then you do not distribute any of these to them ?
No, not as members of farmers' institutes.
Could the minister inform the committee whether he has noticed substantial results from the distribution of these bulletins and other literature of this kind ?

Yes, I think the distribution of this information from the experimental farm has largely aided the development and progress of agriculture, because an immense mass of the most valuable information is thus brought to the notice of the farmers. It does not affect only those who read it; they put it into practice to a certain extent, though not as much as they might do, but still to a certain extent, wherever such work is put into practice, it acts as an object lesson to the surrounding country.
The evidence of all that comes back to you ?
Yes.

In this connection I want to refer again to a recommendation that was made by the committee at the beginning of this session, that a certain

number of copies containing tbe evidence of each of tbe experimental farm bands should be furnished the members to be given out during the session or mailed directly to the farmers, so that they might get it during the current season, evidence on various lines. When that recommendation went out from the committee I drew attention to the fact that in years gone by we found it difficult to get this information in time for the members to distribute it during the session. We can do it then much more easily than we can at home, because we can send it from this House free and without trouble. As yet we have no information that any of these reports have been got out this session. We are drawing near the end of the session, and I am afraid as usual that they may not be received until we have gone home. Now, if they are sent home to us, I have no doubt many members will do in the future as in the past, leave it at their homes during the summer and have it sent back here by mail the next session to be distributed. But in doing that we lose the benefit of having these reports get early into the hands of the farmers containing the information that is useful to them. I would like to suggest to the hon. Minister that he stir up the Printing Bureau to get these reports out at once so that we may distribute them while we are here.

I may perhaps be able to make a little explanation. I happen to be connected with the committee that had to deal with that very matter this session. With the congested state of the Printing Bureau-and anybody who knows anything about printing will know that the Bureau has been much congested-it is absolutely impossible to get out all the reports of parliament while the House is sitting. We have had that matter brought to the attention of the Printing Committee two or three sessions. The Printing Committee has endeavoured to facilitate the issuing of the reports in matters of that kind for the convenience of the House as well as the members, but we found it impossible practically to get all the reports printed in order that the members might avail themselves of the facility of mailing them from the House during the session.
I do not think it is possible to accomplish that under the existing state of affairs at the Bureau. I see there is an item on the paper calling for a grant towards the King's Printer for printing, but it seems to me the only remedy for that difficulty will be to put a large item in the estimates for the enlargement of the Printing Bureau. When that matter comes up I shall have something to say about it. But that is the only remedy, because under existing circumstances the staff of hands at the Bureau cannot be increased, there is a lack of accommodation in the building, the rooms are crowded to the utmost, and a great many Mr. SPROULE.
of the reports that ought to have been out have not yet been issued. That is due to the fact that we have not room in the Bureau to put on an extra staff of hands.
Does the minister know whether these reports can be mailed from our homes free of postage ?
Certainly they can.
I would ask the minister if any appropriation is being made for an experimental fruit farm, either in the Niagara district or anywhere else ?

My hon. friend, I am sure, has already heard of the many requests we have had for branch experimental farms from all parts of the country. I regret to say that there are so many that it would be impossible to satisfy the demands. I think a different system will have to be adopted so as to bring a little more of the experimental work-or of the illustration work, I would prefer to call it-home to the different parts of the country. But to start a larger number of experimental farms than we have now I think would not be possible.

It seems to me the fruit-growing industry deserves the same recognition at the hands of the government as the agricultural industry. Perhaps the fruit industry requires a larger amount of expenditure to make proper experiments than even the farming industry. We have four experimental farms scattered over different parts of the Dominion in different climates, and representing the products of those climates fairly well; but there are none of these farms where experiments can be conducted in regard to fruit that would be of any use to the larger fruit-growing sections. Experiments in fruit are conducted at these farms, it is true, but they are only useful to the northern sections of the Dominion where little fruit is grown. They serve their puipose certainly, I do not wish to detract from the value of these experiments. But there is a much wider field for experiments in fruit-growing that can only be conducted on an experimental farm in a fruit district, either in the Niagara district or somewhere else where fruit is grown on a large scale. We have an example at the present time of the great need of these experiments. We have found that though our fruit is improving from year to year, but on account of our climate and our soil, we cannot export this fruit to a long distance market satisfactorily. People often wonder why the California fruits are shipped here. They see long articles in the Winnipeg and other papers blaming the Ontario fruit packers for the way they pack their fruit. If they only had as much sense as the California

packers, they say, why, they could carry their fruit to long distance markets without trouble. But the fault is not in the packing. There are just as good packers in Ontario as there are in California, and they do their packing just as well, but the climate and soil are of such a character that the fruit will not carry long distances, no matter how hard it is packed, no matter how well it is packed, it will not carry to long distance markets satisfactorily. But there are some varieties of fruit that will carry. I have found in my experience in peaches that there are one or two splendid varieties that will carry to the Northwest Territories or to Europe with every success, they will carry as well as apples. The Elberta variety is one, the Smock is another. The Elberta is one of the finest peaches grown, but they only last a few days. We want a succession of varieties like that, and with experimental fruitgrowing carried on where tests can be made of the different varieties, we would no doubt be able to find out some varieties that would meet the requirements and we would thus be able to secure that splendid Manitoba market Which is perhaps of more use to us, as some gentlemen have said than even the British market, especially for our perishable products. That market is growing at a tremendous rate from year to year, and will absorb all that we can give them in good condition, nearly all the fruit grown in the fruit districts of Ontario. But with the present varieties we cannot do it, except occasionally. The year before last we could ship our plums even as far as Moosomin and Moosejaw, but the next year we couldn't ship them to Winnipeg at all. But if we had the requisite varieties of plums and of peaches we could have shipped them with perfect success. That is one example of the manner an experimental fruit farm would be of great value to the fruit-growers of this country. Fruit-growing is probably one of the main industries of the country, it is worth at . least $15,000,000 a year, equal to the wheat product, equal at least to our export of wheat, and equal'to many of the leading lines of agricultural products that are exported from this country. Year after year it has grown and with proper encouragement, even in a matter of this kind which does not cost very much, it will continue to grow to an enormous extent. I believe we will find, if we are going to ship many of our fruits with success to Europe, that we must learn how to meet the changed conditions. Individuals will find this out in time. It will take many years, but an experimental farm could do it quickly and economically as compared with individual effort. The same argument that applies regarding the usefulness of the experimental farms at Ottawa, in the North-west Territories and in Nova Scotia applies with equal
force to a fruit station which ought to be established in the fruit district.
Carried.

Is the hon. minister not disposed to give some answer to this demand ? Some time ago I asked the hon. minister if it were not possible for us to have an experimental farm, or, at all events, an agricultural school, in the province of Quebec, and he said that he was afraid the resources of the country did not warrant that. It seems to me that the statement of my hon. friend (Mr. Smith, Wentworth) would call for some explanation from the minister. Is it altogether beyond the resources of his department to have such a school established in the Niagara district or in any other part of the country where fruit can be grown with great profit ?

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk), I think, has heard the explanation which I gave not very long ago, that there is a demand from a very large number of sections of Canada for further branch experimental farms. That is the reason of the difficulty in connection with this proposal. The scale upon which the experimental farms have been started in the jdifferent localities is so great that it absorbs the money that is voted for this purpose, and it would absorb it more easily even than it does now if we were to attempt to establish branch experimental farms in larger numbers than we have them now, because we have demands from almost every section of Canada. The hon. gentleman who has just spoken, asks for one in the neighbourhood of Montreal.
I did not ask for an experimental farm, although I think that my hon. friend (Mr. Smith, Wentworth) did.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) asked for a branch experimental farm. I do not know what the hon. gentleman does want if he does not want a branch experimental farm.
I asked for an agricultural college in Quebec.
The hon. gentleman knows perfectly well that the government does not undertake to teach agriculture any more tlmn it undertakes to teach any other subject in the provinces.
I did not know that.

The hon. gentleman knows that educational matters are entirely within the purview of the provinces and that agricultural schools, as other schools, come under the control of the provinces. Several of the provinces, Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have agricultural schools where agriculture is taught in various ways, but, in these Dominion experimental farms, we

do not undertake any teaching at all. It is a matter of experimental work to lind out certain information for the benefit of the farmers and that information is distributed by means of reports and bulletins and the professors from the farms attend agriculture meetings and give information in regard to their work. If we were to try to establish more branch experimental farms it would involve a large expense. I have received demands from Prince Edward Island, from Cape Breton, from the eastern part'of the province of Quebec, from the Lake St. John district especially, from other parts of Quebec, from the part of Ontario which the hon. member for South Wentworth (Mr. Smith, Wentworth) represents, from the Muskoka district, from the new Ontario district, from different parts of Manitoba .and the Northwest Territories and at a little distance from the present experimental farms there, and from half a dozen different places in British Columbia where the people believe that the work of branch experimental farms in their particular neighbourhood would be of great advantage to them. I believe this myself. It is a well-known fact that in the immediate neighbourhood of the experimental farms, agriculture on the whole has made more progress and is perhaps being better carried on than where the farmers cannot easily reach these experimental farms. It was in consequence of that feeling that when the scheme for the establishment of these experimental farms was first brought down to this House, I, as a private member in opposition, objected to the very large scale of these particular experimental farms and I contended that the subject should be dealt with on a smaller scale at each particular farm and that a more extended system of branch farms should be projected. However, that suggestion was not carried out and the farm system as proposed was established at a very heavy cost to the country, a cost which has been well repaid, I believe, because the work, which has been excellent, has been greatly to the advantage of agriculture fn this country. There has been a difference of opinion as to the best way of spending the money that is voted so as to produce the greatest good. I believe to-day that the establishment of illustration stations all over the country, in every county in the Dominion, if possible, where the results of the experimental work at the great farms could be presented as an object lesson to the farmers of the community would be of great advantage. I made a proposition of that kind two or three years ago, but it was not received with favour by the House at that time. Since that time I have received representations from a large number of farmers in the country and from hon. members in this House that they would like to see me introduce that proposition again. They believe it would carry and that it would be acceptable to the great mass of the agriculturists of the country. I believe Mr. FISHER.
myself that possibly something of the kind might well be done to advantage, but I fear that the establishment of some eight or ten, perhaps more, branch farms in addition to those we now have would involve such a large expenditure that it would be impossible to undertake any other work, although, perhaps, this other work would accrue to the general advantage of the farmers and bring more closely home to every district of the country the results of the investigations and experimental work being carried on at the farms. These are the reasons why, so far, I have not seen my way clear to meet the requests for the establishment of further branch experimental farms. There has been a large number of demands, and a large expense would certainly be necessary to comply with all these demands, and if we were to comply with one of them it would be very difficult to refuse the others. The Farm Act to-day establishes five farms, one the central farm, and the four branch ones. That was thoroughly worked out at the time of the inauguration of these farms. I confess that I have not seen my way yet to making an amendment to the Act in the way suggested by the hon. gentleman.

I have thought sometimes that if there could be an arrangement made whereby the various provinces of the Dominion would take a portion of the work and devote their attention to it the usefulness of these farms might be very much extended. In regard to the establishment of fruit stations throughout the country, I think there is one in my riding in the Georgian Bay district, and there is another in Simcoe, the next county east of us. My hon. friend says that one should be established in the Niagara peninsula, or in the Essex district, but I think that these stations might be established in other portions of the country because fruit is grown as successfully almost in every portion of the province, except it may be the peach, as in these districts. The province of Ontario is doing that work now. In connection with the spraying of fruit trees the Dominion is doing something. It seems to me that if some understanding can be reached whereby some portion of the work might be taken up by the province, and another portion by the Dominion, they would not be duplicating the same work and employing a double staff of officials. If that were done they might extend their operations, so as to make them more generally useful to the farmers.

The hon. member for Grey (Mr. Sproule) misunderstands me, if he thinks I suggested any such thing as the illustration station he refers to, in the province of Ontario. I am very well aware there are five or six illustration stations in Ontario in connection with the Guelph Agricultural College, but they are of such a minor character and their reports are distributed in such an ineffective manner, that

they are practically of no use whatever. That is not what we want, but a thorough going experimental farm, such as the central farm here, and the branch farms, which would take up only fruits that are indigenous and can be successfully grown in that particular section of the country. The minister has not made out a case against this by citing the many applications he receives. The climate of the province of Quebec is fairly represented by the Ottawa farm. The climate of Manitoba and the North-west is fairly represented by the farms there. The climate of British Columbia is fairly represented by the one farm, because, as Prof. Saunders says, it is so situated that they have almost all kinds of climate on account of the different elevations. So with Prince Edward Island and the maritime provinces in regard to the Nappan farm. Of course no one can expect a farm for every climate, but there is no farm anywhere in the Dominion which can be useful to the fruitgrowing districts where we grow peaches and plums and grapes successfully. That is a distinct industry and none of our farms are so situated as to fill the want in this respect. Our experimental farms perform good work in ascertaining what fruits can be grown in northern climates where these farms are situated. The Guelph farm is in a section of the country where they cannot grow peaches, plums and grapes as they do in the Niagara district. I submit that we have a good case for the establishment of an experimental farm somewhere in the fruit district. I agree with the minister that a farm in every district would be a great benefit, but of course this is impossible. We cannot have a farm for every locality that differs from the others by even a few degrees of temperature. We have now the various climatic differences fairly well represented by the five farms, in so far as grain raising and stock raising goes, but none of these farms are representatives at all of the climate of southern Ontario, where our commercial peach and plum orchards and vineyards are, and where fall wheat grows with success.
Glasgow Exhibition, $16,000.

When the item of $25,000 was put in the main estimates it was thought that for $40,000 we could make at Glasgow a very creditable showing for Canada. We secured space in the main building, but as the importance of the exhibition came to be recognized, further demands for space were made. Towards the close of the Paris exhibition nearly all the exhibitors asked to have their exhibits sent to Glasgow and we entered into further negotiations to see whether we would be allowed to put up a building on the Glasgow grounds, as we could not otherwise secure more space. We found that we cound not make an exhibit of many important Canadian manufactures unless we did this, and our request was acceded to by the authorities. This building will cost about $14,000 and we have to ask for a supplementary vote. The Glasgow exhibition was opened the other day with great eclat and the reports are that there is a splendid showing of Canadian products and industries.
How many officials have we employed at Glasgow and who are they ?
I think there are eight at present.
Whol are they ?

Col. Wm. O'Brien is the first commissioner. Mr. W. D. Scott, who was one of the commissioners at Paris and who took charge of the transfer of the exhibits to Glasgow and afterwards came here and arranged for further exhibits, has had chief charge of the forwarding and installation of the exhibits. Mr. Brodie is acting as secretary and bookkeeper. Mr. Stewart, who was at Paris, is taking charge of the mineral exhibit. He comes from British Columbia and is well known in mining circles. Mr. Thomas is one of the clerks. Mr. Hamilton, who was at Paris, is also in charge of the fruit exhibit in Glasgow. Mr. Stewart, of Ontario, is at Glasgow in connection with our food products exhibit.
What space have we at Glasgow ?
In the main building we have about 10,000 square feet of floor space and in the Canadian building about 12,000 feet more.
Has the building been erected ?
Yes.
Have you made provision to send fruit this year ?
There is now a fine exhibit of the fruit and apples of last year.

Is the chief commissioner a man who has experience and all the qualifications required for that position. As the minister is aware, our success in these exhibitions in Europe depends a great deal on the experience and qualifications of the chief commissioner. Is it on account of these qualifications that the choice of the minister rested on Col. O'Brien, or, was he recommended to the minister, and if so by whom ?

I cannot say exactly that he was recommended by anybody. I consulted with my colleagues as to our getting a proper representative for Canada at that exhibition. The

name of Col. Wm. O'Brien came to us, and we believed him to be eminently qualified to represent Canada as one who "had taken a large part in the public life of Canada and who knew the country well, and we believed he would make a fitting and worthy representative of the country at the exhibition.
What is his salary ?
It is at the rate of $2,500 a year, the same as the other commissioner's.
And expenses 7
Yes, and an allowance of $5 a day for living expenses, the same rate as is paid to the other exhibition commissioners.

The minister said that Mr. O'Brien's name came to him. I was not quite clear whether Mr. O'Brien brought it or somebody else. Perhaps the hon. gentleman can tell us who brought Mr. O'Brien's name to him.
It floated through the air.

The hen. minister has given Mr. O'Brien an excellent certificate of character, which may be true ; but it would quite surprise moist of the members of this House to learn that Mr. o Brien, though a very estimable gentleman, had any special qualifications for an office of that kind, other than that he was defeated at the last election, and that the hon. gentleman is rewarding him. I would like the minister to tell us what other qualifications he has besides being a defeated candidate.

What steps are taken in the Patent Office to ensure that any one getting out a patent that some one else has not one already for the same article ? I ask this question because last summer, having to negotiate for a patent, I was told by an expert patent lawyer that any one getting out a patent in the United States could rest assured that there was no patent ahead of him for the same article, that if he got his patent he might be safe to go ahead and expend his money; but that in Canada there was not that protection taken, that sometimes a man received a patent for an article and shortly afterwards found 145
that some one else had a patent for practically the same thing.

I think the hon. gentleman must be somewhat mistaken about that. If he can give me instances of that I would be glad to investigate them, but no case of that kind has been brought to my attention. The system here is exactly the same as it is in the United States, except that we do not have as large a staff of examiners, we do not have as large a staff even in proportion to the number of applications for patents. I have been adding to that staff, and I believe I shall have to add still more, because we have not been able to catch up with the work. I have been taking on college graduates, men who have been trained scientifically in the various branches, and I find that these examiners, although young and less experienced, have proved themselves very efficient in the examination of the applications for patents. I propose to continue in that line, because I think it is only right that the very best trained men possible to be found should be employed in this work. It is a very important work, which sometimes involves thousands and hundreds of thousands of dollars of value; because the rejection of a patent might mean ruin to a man, and the acceptance of a patent wrongfully might mean ruin to somebody else. I am glad to know that several times patent solicitors have taken the trouble to compliment the office on the greater efficiency of the work of late, although I am sorry to say that even yet we have not succeeded in getting up the arrears, and getting the work to that point where I would like to see it. I am just now arranging to add another examiner to the staff.

I will remark here that I had occasioh during the session to visit the Patent Office in the interests of some of my friends who are supposed to have great genius, and who desired to acquire patents. I want to state that I found the greatest efficiency. There was no difficulty whatever in getting full information in connection with the matter. I feel perfectly satisfied that the chief, Mr. Lynch, I think it is, has the whole business at his finger's end. There is no difficulty in getting the fullest information concerning patents.

I thank my hon. friend for that tribute to the efficiency of the staff. I think it is only due to the officers who have charge of it.
Quarantine-Public health, $20,000.

The large- increase in this vote is due to the prevalance of smallpox all over the northern part of this continent. Usually our quarantine service is confined to the seaboard, that is to say, we undertake to examine people arriving here on shipboard.



As a general rule the frontier between us and the United States is not watched. But this last year there has been a pretty extensive prevalance of a mild type of smallpox known to the profession as discrete ambulatory smallpox. It is a mild type of disease, so mild that frequently men having it do not even confine themselves to their own homes, but travel about. The results is that it spreads in a most extraordinary way. You will find a little case arising, and a little outbreak hundreds of miles away from any place where it has existed before. The result has been that our people all along the American frontier from east to west, have been asking for protection. I have consulted the Minister of Justice, who informs me that it is my duty as the minister charged with the quarantine service, to protect Canada on our land frontier as well as on our water frontier. I have been obliged to take extraordinary precautions, and to put on a large number of officials to watch the frontier wherever our office has been informed that this disease is prevalent on the other side of the line. In addition to this we have had during the last year to make provisions for some quarantine work in the Yukon territory. People have come in there from the United States, and we have been obliged to establish some quarantine officers there, and I may say that the expense is enormous. That is the reason why I have been obliged to ask this great increase in the quarantine vote.
Do you have to look after the whole frontier ?

Yes, wherever there seems to be disease prevalent on the other side of the line. Dr. Montizambert, the chief of my staff, keeps watch of all that is going on on the other side of the line, and whenever there seems to be an outbreak within reasonable reach of our line, and where people are coming across, then we watch the avenues.
Have you a station at North Bay, or in the Georgian Bay district, or in the lumber camps, where it appears to be quite prevalent.

Yes, at Sault Ste. Marie. Port Arthur, Thes-salon, I think at Collingwood, and other places.
Towards the prevention of the spread of tuberculosis in cattle, $10,000.
I would like to ask the hon. minister if this vote includes such officials as Mr. Stubbs, who has been appointed in Ontario ?

By the arrangement which I made quite recently with the American authorities, the only certificates which can be received at the frontier for the test of cattle going across the frontier are those of my permanent officials. By the former arrangement the American authorities accepted the certificates given by a veterinary in Canada whose name we submitted to them, and from time to time, as occasion required, we submitted a large number of names. The American authorities had experienced some difficulties in connection with the importation of tuberculosis cattle from Europe. They made a new arrangement in connection with the testing of cattle in England, and they included Canada in this new arrangement, abrogating entirely the former arrangement. The new plan was that they should send one of their officei's into Canada to test any animals intended for export to the Uuited States. Our breeders felt this to be a great injustice, and a. hindrance to the export trade, and I was asked to try to modify it. I first of all entered into correspondence with the Washington authorities, pointing out that it was in contravention of the former arrangement, and asking them to modify it. I went down to Washington and spent a day in consultation with the Minister of Agriculture and the head of his bureau, and they agreed to accept, not the tests made by any Canadian veterinary, but the tests made by any permanent officer of my department.

There have been three or four new appointments made. I gave the names of my officers who are already on me staff, but in consequence of the large proportion of the export trade, particularly in Ontario, I found that my ordinary officers could not undertake that work, and, therefore, I appointed Mr. Stubbs, to make his headquarters at Toronto, and be on hand for it. Ever since the appointment he has been at it day after day without interruption.
Are there any others besides Mr. Stubbs ?

Mr. Stubbs is the only one in Ontario. There was an officer appointed in Manitoba, not on salary, but on fees, because the export trade is comparatively small, and he is to be paid according to the work he does. There has been another appointment in the Territories to do this work, and any other veterinary work that we may require. We have had a good many demands in different parts of the Territories on account of what I may call local outbreaks of disease amongst cnttle. do that work, and we have been employing- men for a year past to go to certain places, and we have paid them for their time. Mr. Stubbs's appointment was made on my own recommendation, from knowing that gentleman for many years as an efficient and accomplished veterinarian, a man who had experience of this kind of work. His salary is $1,200 a year, and his travelling-expenses are paid when he is away from home.

The hon. minister has stated that Mr. Stubbs's appointment has been made by reason of the fact of his long-acquaintance with Mr. Stubbs, and by reason of the fact of Mr. Stubbs's connection with this class of business. I do not know how long the hon. minister has known Mr. Stubbs. He comes from the part of the country where I reside, and I certainly never heard of Mr. Stubbs being an authority on cattle. He has some qualifications as a trotting horseman and a politician. I suppose that his name came in like that of Col. O'Brien, that it was just wafted in by somebody, and that his qualifications for the position were simply those of political exigencies. As I understand it he is placed in a very important position. Mr. J. E. Blackball, of Clinton, is president of the local Conservative association. Mr. Blackhall is also a member of the Ontario Veterinary College. It is very extraordinary the confidence that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Holmes) has in Conservatives just now. I am sure that gentleman would be greatly flattered to know that he was singled out by 145J
the hon. gentleman to give him a certificate on behalf of Mr. Stubbs. Why did not the hon. gentleman give some better reason than the title tattle of some gentleman whom he calls a Conservative, than the statement that Conservatives generally approve of it ?
I do not know that the approval of a Conservative, or of the individual who is just named by the hon. gentleman, has anything to do -with it. It is perfectly plain to the country that Mr. Stubbs is one of the lame ducks that had to be taken care of. However, I am not going to pursue that subject.
I am going to ask the hon. Minister of Agriculture whether the United States government abrogated the arrangement that the hon. gentleman concluded shortly after he came into office and entered into new quarantine regulations with Great Britain ignoring entirely the interests of Canada. Perhaps I did' not quite catch the meaning of the hon. gentleman's statement. The meaning I took was that the former arrangement made for the entry of cattle going from Canada into the United States was that the United States authorities were prepared to take certificates of such persons as might be named by the Canadian government or the minister himself. I understood the minister to state that the reason the United States refused to take such certificates, was because a new arrangement had been entered into with the mother country entirely ignoring the interests of Canada.

The hon. gentleman did not quite understand me. In 1897 I made an arrangement with the Washington authorities which included a promise to accept the tuberculin test certificate of any Canadian veterinarian whose name was suggested to the Department of Agriculture at Washington by the Department of Agriculture in Ottawa. I gave the names of large numbers of veterinarians all over the Dominion, whom I believed to be competent, and numbers of them were recommended by the importers, because they were employed by the importers in other work and the arrangement was found very convenient. That worked all right for a long time. The American authorities began to test cattle coming from Europe and they found that frequently the certificates as to animals coming from Great Britain, very incorrect on the face of them.
Is not that the experience of Canada ?

To a certain extent it is. The United States authorities then issued a regulation applying to all foreign countries, refusing to accept the certificate of any foreign veterinarian and only accepting a certificate of the test made by one of their own officers. They named an official at Buffalo who would come to Canada to make the test. It was a great hardship to our exporters. It is well known that the great province of Ontario

is a breeding ground of thoroughbred cattle, I might almost say for the world, certainly for the American continent, and I am glad to say that American buyers come over and take our cattle and make a profitable . trade for our people. The exporters appealed to me to try and remove the difficulty.
11 succeeded in inducing the American authorities to issue a new regulation by which the certificate of permanent officers of the Canadian Department of Agriculture would be accepted just as certificates from their own officers. They went so far as to agree that an officer whom I have sent to England to do this work for Canada-as the United States authorities have sent an officer to England to test cattle for them-should have power to issue a certificate which would be accepted by the United States authorities on the arrival of cattle here. I reciprocated by accepting the certificate of the United States officer in England for cattle coming to Canada.
Has the minister an officer in England ?

Yes, lately sent over.
Mr-. CLANCY. What is his name ?
Mr. Rutherford.
Another lame duck.
He is not a lame duck by any means.

There are others.

Portage la Prairie.

No.

Yes. It was in consequence of that I decided to send a Canadian officer to make the test in England. It is true that the United States authorities did away with the acceptance of the certificates of our veterinarians, but that regulation applies to the rest of the world as well as to Canada. When representations were made to them that this was unfair to us, they said they were just as willing to accept the test of our permanent officers as of their own permanent officers and they put us practically on the same plane as themselves. The complaint arose entirely from what were said to be unsatisfactory tests of cattle imported from Great Britain. I have never understood very clearly whether it was because of the insufficiency of the test, or the want of qualification on the part of the person making it. I am led to believe that very unsatisfactory tests have been made by persons of great skill and experience. There was no complaint with regard to the veterinarians in Canada. rangement made by him, and laid down the rule, and it could not be expected that they would lay down any different rule for Canada from what they had for themselves. The hon. gentleman may say the people should be allowed to do unwise things; but it is not for the hon. gentleman to provide them with all the facilities for doing unwise things ; and this is what he did in that case. As experience tries the hon. gentleman's plan, I fear that it will not be generally approved. But I come back to the question I started with: does the continuance of the tuberculin test as now carried on meet with general favour at the hands of the stock-breeders in Canada ? The hon. gentleman did not answer that.

I cannot say what universal favour it meets with. I know that a large number of the leading farmers of this country believe in the tuberculin test and want to see it continued and encouraged in the country. There are a few people who discredit it, and are afraid of it. At the same time, I am satisfied that the results of the work in connection with this test in Canada and elsewhere, have been to contribute to the general improvement of the live stock affected by it. I am satisfied that to-day the tuberculin test in Canada is making progress and meeting with favour amongst the people of the country, although I grant that there are men who dispute its efficacy, and are not willing to have it applied to their animals, just as there are people in the country who object to vaccination, although the consensus of opinion in the country favours it.

Surely the hon. gentleman is not putting it on the ground of prejudice
like the opposition to vaccination. The farmers of this country will not be satisfied with the hon. gentleman's statement that opposition to the tuberculin test must have grown out of stupidity or prejudice. Is it not a fact that it has been on trial long enough ? Is it not a fact that the hon. gentleman has had protests against it on the ground that it was injurious to the country ? Is it not a fact that at a very influential convention of breeders at Chicago some very strong ground was taken against it about a year ago 1 I think I may go further, and state that the Minister of Agriculture of the great province of Ontario does not quite share the hon. gentleman's view. He may find that after all he has a very small following in his contention. If the objection to the tuberculin test is founded on no better ground than the narrow ground of prejudice, such as some people have against vaccination, it would be the duty of the hon. gentleman and his department to take some means to remove that prejudice.

We are taking the best means we can to meet and combat it, as well as to find out its existence. The tuberculin test is merely a method of finding out whether the disease is present or not. That is what it is used for. The other part of the work connected with tuberculosis is that of spreading information through the country, and leading the farmers to keep their stock in better sanitary conditions, so that they will be less liable to disease, and more likely to resist it successfully if it appears among them.

Has the hon. gentleman made any provision, other than where animals are found to be diseased in a herd, to quarantine them, and either kill them or allow them to die by the slow process of the disease ?
We do not compel slaughter.

The hon. gentleman does not compel slaughter, for the simple reason, which he has stated before in the House, that the government do not propose to make themselves liable for compelling slaughter. Does the hon. gentleman not think that we have come to a time when this country can afford, in the general interest of the country, to spend some money in slaughtering all animals known to be diseased ? It seems an extraordinary thing that in a country so great as Canada, with all its great possibilities, the people are almost intoxicated with expenditures in other quarters, while in the very necessary direction I have indicated not a cent is expended. I am surprised that the hon. gentleman has not a dollar to spare for the purpose of slaughtering those animals known to be diseased. Owing to the selfish desire, which of course

is natural, of persons owning stock, to keep the animal quarantined for months in the hope that it may recover, the possibilities of thei spread of the disease are much increased. In some very exceptional cases, the animals have recovered, but as a rule they die, and it would have been much better to slaughter them in the first instance.

A good deal of dissatisfaction has been expressed by importers with regard to the tuberculin test. No doubt the hon. gentleman heard something of these complaints when he visited the show at Guelph. Has he decided to make any change in the regulations regarding tlie importation of cattle .and the use of the tuberculin test ?

I have sent an officer to England to make the test there, for importers object to its being applied after the animals have crossed the ocean. We still apply the test to cattle coming in from the old country and the United States and elsewhere, which have not been tested previously. But cattle that have been tested by our own officer, we do not test any further. The officer furnishes a certificate, which is quite sufficient.

Is it not a fact that the importers object to the test entirely as being actually injurious and not always reliable. I have seen some reports from leading authorities to this effect. Is the hon. gentleman convinced that amongst the ablest modern, authorities the opinion is that the test is reliable ?

Yes, the most reputable authorities who have thoroughly investigated this question, say that the test is reliable and does not injure the animals except in very rare cases in which the conditions are exceptional. Instances have been given, where impotency has been present after the test, but that was no doubt due to other causes, because such result has not followed the vast majority of cases in which the test has been applied. And especially is this true when I find, as a matter of fact, that other countries which buy cattle in the old country are applying this test. Argentine tests all cattle going to Argentine, and the United States tests all cattle going to that country. If a British breeder cannot send to either of these countries animals which cannot stand the test, he will send them to Canada, and we shall be practically a dumping ground for all the tuberculous animals which British breeders want to export.

Canada would be free to buy or to refuse to buy. It is not the part of the breeders to send them without finding a purchaser here. If the minister would modify his statement and, instead of saying that this Is a thoroughly reliable test, say that it is a valuable test, I would Mr. CLANCY.
agree with him. Looking up the authorities, for, as a professional man I take sufficient interest in them to go over them, I see quite a number of important articles from eminent men in that line who assert that it did produce injurious results on tlie line I have suggested, and that it was not a thoroughly reliable test. I think the hon. minister will admit that, in the United States, where they have applied the test to many animals it has been found that there is no relationship between the rise of temperature and the disease-in an animal slightly affected the temperature will occasionally go very high, while in others where the disease is in the advanced stage the rise in temperature is very slight.

That is true.
Mr. SPROULE-while in Other cases where the disease is very bad there is only indifferent or a slight rise of temperature.
That is true.

Therefore, the test is not thoroughly reliable in that respect. Has the hon. minister succeeded in allaying the fears of cattle exporters ? Some time ago there was a good deal of feeling amongst them on this subject, Hon. John Dryden stating that if this was to be enforced he would go out of the business, while others of almost equally extensive experience backed him up. It would seem that there has been general dissatisfaction and there was a strong demand for some change. This taken in connection with the fact that, as I believe, it has been proven pretty conclusively that this test is not thoroughly reliable though, in the main, it is the best test we know of-and with the further fact that it has been repeatedly alleged by eminent veterinarians that it produces some of the deleterious effects that I have mentioned-indicates it would be worth while to collect these data very carefully and to advance cautiously.

Since the meeting at Guelph and the discussion that took place in the newspapers at that time, about the time of my visit to Washington, a deputation of breeders of Ontario came to my office and I explained what I was doing. They said that while they would like me to get the entire absolution of the test on going into the United States, they were pleased with what I had secured; and they said that the sending of a veterinarian to England for my department was a concession they valued, and they were much gratified with the arrangements made.
It is much better than it was.

I do not say that it is perfect.

Has the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fisher) renewed his efforts for the removal of the embargo on Canadian cattle going into Great Britain ? I should think that the hon. minister should have two strong reasons to urge. One is the overflowing gratitude wrhich we are told possesses the British heart, leading the English consumer to seek Canadian products. The other is seen in the hon. gentleman's statement that a large number of diseased cattle are coming from Great Britain to Canada
I did not say that.
The hon. gentleman said that very unsatisfactory tests-
I did not say that large numbers of diseased cattle were coming from Great Britain to Canada.
Well, we will minimize that to suit the hon. gentleman's position.
I said that some have come.
And more will come.
Possibly.
And the hon. gentleman suggested that we must keep up the test on cattle to be exported to Canada, or this country would be made the dumping ground for the diseased cattle of Great Britain.
No doubt.
In view of these statements, has the hon. gentleman turned his efforts in the directions of having the embargo removed ?

I have made efforts in that direction and am continuing to do so. I have to-day pre pared a despatch to the Imperial authorities which I hope to send by the mail this week, and I hope, when I go to England, as I shall shortly, to still further enforce the arguments, I think are very strong, in favour of removing that embargo from our cattle. I can assure my hon. friends I shall make representations as strong as I can, enforced and backed up by the feeling of all Canadians that not only is this an unfair thing itself, but that it is an unjust aspersion upon the health of our Canadian cattle. I made many representations on the subject when I was in England before. I interviewed the Minister of Agriculture and urged upon him with all my force the need of a change. Nothing resulted. I cannot tell whether anything will result from the efforts I shall make this year. But I shall use every argument,
and I think that our arguments are so strong that they cannot be met by argument, but they may be met by inaction.

Perhaps the hon. minister forgets that in Great Britain the farmers are becoming more and more protectionist. This may be one of the instruments of protection used by the British farmer to keep his own market for his own cattle. And the hon. gentleman will see more things like that going on there. The recent budget is said to have been a free trade budget, but on examination it will be found to have marked protectionist features. This embargo is not a question of the health of cattle, but it is part of a protectionist and agrarian movement in the interests of agriculture in England. It is just one of the indications that may be seen in England that they are coming to the protectionist view of things and that they are going to begin by protecting their own agriculture.

I would like to give some of the latest authorities on a subject of tuberculosis in Canada, but I will confine myself to one, the latest American authority :
The work began on November 21, 1894, and the record for fourteen weeks to March 1, 1895, shows 4,226 animals tested and 250 condemned. Of these 14-8 per cent failed to show evidence of the diease at the post mortems.
Then he goes on and says that in 85'2 per cent of the cases tested where there was evidence of disease, they turned out on the post mortem examinations to show evidence of diseasei
The counties of Nantucket and Dukes have been completed. A total of 1,837 animals have been tested in these two counties, with but seven condemned, all of which proved diseased on post mortem. In addition to the seven condemned on the two islands, seven other animals were bought and killed because of physical indications which induced the agents of the board to withhold the brand of soundness. None of these last, however, proved to be tuberculous.
So, it is quite clear that it is not altogether a reliable test, but, it is perhaps the best one we have up to the present.
Mounted Police-Amount required to complete service of the year, $60,000.

The other day, on the estimates for the coming year, I stated that we would have to increase our estimates liv $60,000, and bring the sum up to the neighbourhood of $400,000. The force is estimated to he of 500 men, and we have reached the conclusion by experience that under the present condition of things it is impossible to keep up the force at a less cost than $800 for a man and horse. The force is distributed over territory 700 miles in .extent. We have over seventy stations, from the limits of the boundary of Manitoba to the Saskatchewan river, and up to the Mac-

kenzie river. This year we extended our patrol even to the mouth of the Mackenzie river. For the information of hon. gentle-linen, I have had a map prepared which shows the extent of our patrol and of the territory we have to cover.

I would ask the right hon. gentleman if he has had brought to his notice some complaints that were made on behalf of the young men who have within the last year enlisted, by reason of being compelled, owing to an old regulation, to pay themselves the cost of transportation. It is desirable to get a good class of men, we must elect from the best specimens of young men in the country. They are not overpaid, I think. It seems to me a niggardly thing that persons enlisting, ,fior instance in the city of London or the town of Chatham, where my attention has been called to some cases, should be obliged to pay the cost of transportation to the ,North-west, and at the same time to pay some share of their outfit. I desire to ask the right hon. gentleman if any cases of that kind have been brought to his notice ?

I must say that I have not heard of any complaints of the nature the hon. gentleman refers to. The regulation is that the applicants who are admitted to the force pay their fares to headquarters at Regina, but they have to pay nothing for their outfit. The regulation has been in existence for many years.
I have been informed from reliable quarters that they have to pay a portion of their outfit. t
No. Could my hon. friend give me any particular case ?
I have a letter which I will hand to the right hon. gentleman so that he can see the nature of the complaints.
What is the strength of the force now ?

Five hundred men in the North-west Territories and 250 in the Yukon. With reference to the complaint mentioned by the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) I may say that if there have been any complaints they are very few. The force has been in existence (now for 20 years, and the regulations at present were in existence before I came into the department.

Is this amount of $60,000 applicable to the increase in the Yukon ?
The PRIME MINISTER, No, only for the North-west Territories.
What additional number of men does it represent ?
It represents no additional number of men. When we came into office the number of men was a

We have had to spend a good ideal in transportation to and fro, taking men from the different stations, bringing them here, equipping them and sending them to their destination. But doing the best we can, we cannot maintain the force with less than $800 for man and horse. There are about 400 horses. We think that in course of time we shall be able to reduce the expenditure down to a little under $800.

The circumstances afford a good argument for the erection of one or more new provinces in the North-west. I hope the right hon. gentleman will bear that in mind. Why this government has not established at least one new province in the North-west long ago, I cannot understand. If we had one or more provinces up there the duty of policeing the territory would devolve upon the provinces instead of upon the Dominion.
The hon. gentleman is too previous. The suggestion may be a good one, but we are taking a census this year, and we had better wait until the census is known before we carve out any new provinces.

I do not understand from the explanations of the right hon. gentleman how men enlisting with the constabulary to South Africa would cause so much additional expense. I can understand that we should have some additional expense in that connection, but with the increase in the number of men $60,000 seems to be a considerable jump.

If my hon. friend looks at the figures he will see in the comparison that there is an explanation for it. In 1896-7 the expense of the force was $504,000, in 1897-8 $369,000, in 1898-9 $402.000, in 1899-1900 $351,000. That year and the year before we had incidents occurring which rather demoralized the force. We had to take from the force 250 men and send them to the Yukon, and then we had

to take 200 men and send them to South Africa. We had to replace these men, we had to send them to Regina and then to send them out to the depots where they were stationed. That entailed a great deal of transportation which we did not have the previous year, and therefore, it is not extraordinary that we should have incurred a greater expenditure, which, under normal conditions, we should not have incurred.
How many new stations have been established ?

I should say ten or twelve.

In regard to the complaint respecting the paper combine, the information furnished by the Canadian Press Association seemed to be sufficient to call for an investigation in the manner prescribed by what might be called the Combine Clause in the Tariff Act of 1897. A reference of the matter was made in the terms of tlie Act to Mr. Justice Tas-chereau of the Superior Court of the province of Quebec. He has been in Ottawa to make some arrangement in the matter and has intimated that he will be prepared to enter into the inquiry within a very few days. Due notice will be given by publication in the Canada Gazette in order that the matter may have an official stamp, and no doubt the gentlemen who made the complaint will be prepared to bring forward witnesses.
Is it the intention of the government to rely on those who made the complaint to supply the evidence ?
The gentlemen who made the complaint volunteered that they were ready to supply the evidence, and we shall await their action.
I read somewhere that they were not disposed to do that now, but wished to put the onus on the government. I would like to have that question cleared up.

At the time the very large delegation waited on us no question of the kind was raised. All these gentlemen asked was that the machinery of the Tariff Act might be put in operation. What the government do in this matter is simply to appoint the tribunal and then it is open to all persons interested to present their claims. I may say that I was called upon within' the last day or so by gentlemen connected with the Canadian Press Association, who put some questions to me in regard to that matter. They were aware that they would have to accept a very serious responsibility, but I do not know that they were not willing to accept it; and when Judge Taschereau opens his

court, I have no doubt they will be present and will be prepared to produce such evidence as they can in support of their allegations.
Have any other complaints been made to the government with regard to other combines, and if so, is it the intention of the government to have them investigated ?

Each one of these cases will have to be investigated on its merits. I think I am correct in stating that of late no other complaint has been made on which action could be taken. A year or more ago some complaint was made to us, but in the judgment of the government the evidence supplied was not sufficient to make out a case. I had one letter referred to me by one of my colleagues recently, but it did not furnish sufficient information to become the basis of further action.
I hold in my hand a number of letters with reference to the leather combine, which I have already dealt with in this House, and as to which I know that representations were made to the government.
I said that there were some matters a year or so ago. That is what my hon. friend refers to.

This matter was gone into carefully, amongst others, by Mr. Gar-row, an eminent lawyer in the west, and he came to the conclusion that there was a most effective combine in that line, and one most injurious to the small tanners of the country. I hold in my hand a letter from Getty & Scott, of Galt, in answer to a letter from Mr. Smith, of Goderich, asking for information on the subject. In this letter they say :
We have Mr. Blackwell, formerly of the Stratford Shoe Company, cutting stock for us, and he informs us that you have an oak tanned stock which is very suitable for our work. While we are on the manufacturers' list of the Tanners' Association, yet if we can get a good line of stock, and at prices that would pay us to do so, we would not hesitate to break away, as the whole thing is systematic stealing.

Only a few large firms make the Spanish-tanned leather ; and a number of men who deal In leather have entered into an agreement that they will buy all their stock from those parties who are in the combine, because by doing that they get a rebate of 5 per cent on all purchases.
